job.style: a news-style report about a real-world situation

passage: In a recent community health drive, local experts clarified several myths about microorganisms. While many people fear that all microbes are harmful, most are actually essential for life. For instance, decomposers break down dead leaves into nutrients that enrich the soil, ensuring matter is recycled rather than lost. In the medical field, doctors emphasized that antibiotics are specifically designed to fight bacterial infections, not viral illnesses like the common cold or flu. Furthermore, vaccines act as a preventative measure to train our immune system before we get sick, rather than serving as a cure for someone already showing symptoms. Experts also addressed food safety, noting that pasteurization heats milk to kill harmful pathogens, yet some harmless microbes still remain. Finally, they explained that plants cannot absorb nitrogen directly from the air; instead, they rely on specialized bacteria in the soil to fix nitrogen into a usable form. Understanding these roles helps us appreciate that microbes are not just germs, but vital partners in our ecosystem and health.

items.evidence: For instance, decomposers break down dead leaves into nutrients that enrich the soil, ensuring matter is recycled rather than lost.
items.q: A dead leaf rots away on the ground. Where does its matter go?
options: It becomes nutrients that enrich the soil
It turns into nothing and vanishes
It becomes gas that rises into the air
It stays in the leaf but turns black
items.explain: Decomposers break dead leaves into nutrients for the soil, so the matter is recycled, not lost.

wrong.why: thinks all rotting matter leaves as gas
thinks rotting only changes colour, not matter

items.evidence: In the medical field, doctors emphasized that antibiotics are specifically designed to fight bacterial infections, not viral illnesses like the common cold or flu.
items.q: Meena has a cold caused by a virus. What would antibiotics do for her?
options: They would not help against the virus
They would cure it within a day
They would train her body against it
They would kill the virus but not bacteria
items.explain: Antibiotics fight bacterial infections, not viral illnesses like the common cold, so they would not help.

wrong.why: thinks antibiotics treat colds and flu
thinks antibiotics strengthen the immune system
thinks viruses are a type of bacteria

items.evidence: Furthermore, vaccines act as a preventative measure to train our immune system before we get sick, rather than serving as a cure for someone already showing symptoms.
items.q: Why is a vaccine given to a healthy child?
options: It prepares the body before illness begins
It removes the illness the child already has
It kills bacteria that are already inside
It makes the child sick for a short time
items.explain: Vaccines prevent disease by training the immune system before sickness, not by curing people already ill.

wrong.why: thinks vaccines are a cure for current disease
mixes vaccines up with antibiotics that kill bacteria
thinks vaccines work by causing illness first

items.evidence: Finally, they explained that plants cannot absorb nitrogen directly from the air; instead, they rely on specialized bacteria in the soil to fix nitrogen into a usable form.
items.q: How does a bean plant get the nitrogen it needs to grow?
options: Soil bacteria change nitrogen into a usable form
Its leaves take nitrogen gas from the air
Its roots pull nitrogen gas straight from the soil
Rainwater carries nitrogen directly into its stem
items.explain: Plants cannot use nitrogen from air; bacteria in the soil change it into a form plants can use.

wrong.why: thinks leaves absorb nitrogen gas from air
thinks nitrogen only works near roots without bacteria
guesses rain delivers nitrogen to the plant
